newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Vereinsbank CEO sees profits, share price up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Vereinsbank CEO sees profits, share price up.

text.p: The head of Bayerische Vereinsbank AG on Tuesday said the bank remained on track for profits to rise at least 10 percent this year and that its shares were substantially undervalued.

Albrecht Schmidt, chief executive of Germany's fourth largest commercial bank, also told Reuters he did not see the bank as being at risk of a hostile takeover after merger rumours drove Vereinsbank shares sharply higher last year.
Noting that Vereinsbank shares had stalled since March at between 70 and 74 marks, Schmidt said: "I consider a share price of 80 marks to be a correct valuation."

While a precise forecast for full year earnings was not possible, Schmidt said: "It is clear that we are not above plans in terms of risk provisions, an area in which we are always very cautious. We are working towards double-digit profit growth."

Vereinsbank posted an 18.7 percent rise in first quarter operating profit before risk provisions to 614.7 million marks ($355.7 million). In 1996, operating profit after risk provisions rose by 18.4 percent to 1.636 billion marks.
The mortgage specialist's shares ended bourse trade on Tuesday barely changed at 71.95 marks.
Taking a by now familiar line among German financial industry leaders, Schmidt played down talk of an imminent shake-up in the German banking landscape.
Hostile mergers would not work in what is traditionally a consensus-driven environment, he said, and Vereinsbank itself was not actively seeking a partner.
"The profile of the bank is far more important than its size," he said. "It makes no sense to become larger and weaker."

Vereinsbank has been at the centre of merger speculation in Germany since last July when market leader Deutsche Bank AG revealed it had built up a 5.21 percent stake in the Bavarian mortgage lending specialist.
But Schmidt said that for a merger to work in Germany, extensive preparation had to be done and the participants in the alliance would have to match in terms of corporate culture.
On Deutsche's plans for its stake in Vereinsbank, Schmidt would only say: "Deutsche has thrown its hat into the ring."
He cited ABN-AMRO in the Netherlands and Chase Manhattan Corp in the U.S. as examples of how bank mergers could actually work.
Speaking on the fringes of the International Monetary Conference in Switzerland, Schmidt said Vereinsbank's focus for the future would be on maximising productivity and expanding key business areas.
On personnel, Schmidt said he did not envisage major staff cuts, but rather expected employees to be flexible.
"Cutting staff is not a dominant topic for us," he said.
On the recently vexed question of whether Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is on track to get off the ground on time in 1999, Schmidt said he was confident of a timely start.
"We are looking at the frame, not at the picture and the picture is one of a converging Europe," he said.
